title: Throughput-oriented design over single-thread performance
where_in_paper: Introduction / design philosophy / commercial workload characteristics
decision: Optimize the entire microarchitecture for aggregate throughput (performance/Watt) on commercial server workloads rather than single-thread ILP or high frequency.
alternatives_or_rejected: Conventional high-ILP, deeply pipelined, high-frequency cores designed first for single-thread performance and later extended with limited multithreading (the approach attributed to contemporary desktop-oriented designs).
rationale: Commercial server applications exhibit high thread-level parallelism, low ILP, high cache-miss rates, and many unpredictable branches; data-center power, cooling, and space constraints make performance/Watt the primary metric.
outcome: A 32-thread design that hides memory and pipeline stalls via thread overlap, delivering high throughput at modest frequency and power (~70 W class).

title: Simple single-issue cores rather than complex ILP cores
decision: Use simple, single-issue, six-stage in-order pipelines (UltraSPARC-II style) with minimal speculation, maximizing the number of cores and threads that fit on the die.
alternatives_or_rejected: Out-of-order, superscalar, or heavily speculative cores that would consume far more area and power per thread.
rationale: Simple pipelines allow many cores to be integrated; resource sharing across threads re-uses execution units and caches, improving area and power efficiency while still exploiting the abundant TLP of server workloads.
outcome: Eight cores on a single die, each supporting four threads, for 32 hardware threads total; high pipeline utilization (reported IPC near 6 out of a maximum of 8 on SpecJBB-class work).

title: Four threads per core with fine-grain interleaving
decision: Support four hardware threads per core with zero-cost fine-grain interleaving (instructions from ready threads selected each cycle); unique per-thread state (registers, instruction/store buffers) but shared pipeline, caches, and TLBs.
alternatives_or_rejected: Fewer threads per core (or single-threaded cores) that would leave the pipeline idle on stalls, or coarser-grain switching.
rationale: Multiple threads hide both memory latency and pipeline stalls; when one thread misses or stalls, others continue, keeping the simple pipeline busy and maximizing outstanding memory references.
outcome: Effective latency hiding and high pipeline efficiency without complex speculation; area overhead of four threads reported as modest (~20 % on an already small core).

title: Shared, highly associative, banked L2 and high-bandwidth memory system
where_in_paper: Memory subsystem / L2 and DRAM interface
decision: Provide a single shared 3 MB L2 (4-way banked, 12-way associative) connected by a high-bandwidth crossbar, plus multiple DDR2 channels delivering >20 GB/s, rather than large private L2s per core.
alternatives_or_rejected: Large private per-core caches that would reduce sharing efficiency and consume more area for the same total capacity.
rationale: Server workloads have large working sets and benefit from data sharing; a shared L2 with high associativity mitigates conflict misses from 32 threads, while banking and the crossbar supply the bandwidth needed to keep many outstanding misses in flight.
outcome: Sufficient bandwidth and low-enough latency to sustain high aggregate IPC; measured L2 and memory latencies that still allow ~70 % pipeline efficiency under commercial load.

title: Single shared FPU across all cores
decision: Implement only one floating-point unit shared by all eight cores rather than a private FPU per core.
alternatives_or_rejected: Per-core FPUs that would increase die area and power for workloads that are integer-dominated.
rationale: Commercial server applications (databases, web, Java) are overwhelmingly integer; a single shared FPU is sufficient and saves substantial area and power.
outcome: Area and power efficiency prioritized for the target throughput workloads; floating-point performance intentionally de-emphasized.
